15 New Tarmac Works Collectibles You Can Buy Today
44 photos
Photo: Tarmac Works
I’m facing a “huge” dilemma. You could say it’s a first-world problem, as I realize it’s not something most people would be concerned about. I’m working with a designer to find the best solution for my new office/man cave. It’s not a huge room, and I want it to integrate three of my hobbies plus the work side of things.
I’ve mentioned I want some sort of display for my motorcycle helmets, racing memorabilia, and diecast collectibles. I’ve been thinking about those wall-mounted display cases as an option, and I’m starting to think I should keep brands separate. Hot Wheels and Matchbox would be on one side, Mini GT and Kaido House on another, then there’s the Tarmac Works area, but what about my Kyosho, Tomica and Solido cars?
It’s even more complicated with the latter as they’re all 1/18th-scale models. I could make things simple and just keep 50 collectibles total and organize them by theme: JDM, Drifting, Racing, Supercars or something along those lines. Right now I’m almost buried in tiny cars, as I’ve been actively ordering dozens of them again.
I’m currently trying to bring my Mini GT line-up up to par with the Tarmac Works models I’ve unboxed this year. And there’s this voice inside my head that keeps pushing me to join the TW Owners Club, if only to get access to the TWOC Members Only Models (a minimum of two per year). The final November pre-order went live about a week ago, and I signed up for both of the two Ferraris.
However, if you need some new cars to enjoy before Christmas, the November release features a line-up of 15 vehicles to choose from. The Porsche 911 GT3 R is the largest of them all, as it’s a 1/43rd-scale item. It’s also the most expensive one here at $46.90 before taxes. I believe it had a MoonEyes themed livery the first time we saw it, too, and I prefer that black and yellow look over the new version.
There’s a new 1/43rd-scale Porsche in town! Photo: Tarmac Works This thing reportedly weighs 1.1 lbs/0.5 kg, and that makes me curious to see how it compares to Mattel’s Premium 1/43rd-scale models. I’m quite excited to see the Vertex Toyota Aristo JZS161, mainly because it’s an HKS/Taniguchi special model. This casting was just recently available as a MOM release for $12.90. Production was limited to 768 units, and there’s even a Chrome Chase version to look for if you’re interested in that sort of thing.
I’m doing my best to expand my D1GP collection, and Tarmac Works has been an incredible source for that in recent years. And the latest drop is solid proof for that, as the URAS Skyline ER34 is making its debut in the Global64 series. Uras is basically “Monkey” spelled backwards in Japanese, and you might remember how silly Ken Nomura used to act during D1GP events.
It’s safe to assume some of the iconic liveries he used over the years will make their way into the 1/64th-scale Universe thanks to Felix and his team in Hong Kong. The First Edition of the ER34 casting still looks great in plain blue, and this time I’m curious to get a closer look at the Chrome Blue chase. You can also opt for the blister version of the collectible if you enjoy displaying it that way.
Speaking of Nissan Skylines , the John Sibal-designed, widebody R32 is now available with a new look. It’s another artistic project in collaboration with Sean Wotherspoon, which reminds me of the Hot Wheels Deora Mattel released not long ago. I unboxed both the Millennium Jade and Greddy variations of the casting in June this year and it is without doubt one of the nicer R32s you can find on the market. Still, because of this iteration’s special nature, it can cost between $19.90 and $36.90 before tax.
Chase model takes a different route Photo: Tarmac Works I would rather go after something else within that same budget instead. For the Porsche 928 S you can also opt between the regular packaging and the blister card which is nice. The reason why there are two cars in some of the presentation photos might not be so obvious, as it’s a game of “spot the differences”. Look at the headlights!
The one with the pop-up headlights is the Chase version, so there’s no livery change here. I think it’s a fairly creative way of doing things, even though some people might not enjoy it as much. The funny part is that I believe the original, First Edition of the casting had it the other way around. That car featured a simple, red paint job, and it also lacked the Safety Car lights we now have on this iteration.
It’s the kind of flexibility you’ll often see at Tarmac Works and it makes collecting these cars all the more enjoyable. The Ford Mustang GTD has been out for a few years now and it makes perfect sense that multiple scale model car manufacturers have created replicas of it. You can’t expect a $2 Hot Wheels to look like a $11.90 version of the American machine from Tarmac Works though. It’s part of the Global64 series, where you’ll also find the Shelby GT350R/GT4.
I believe this is just the second iteration of the casting, as the previous one was red with black stripes down the middle. One of my local dealers has a 25% discount for it, which says a lot about how popular the model was where I live. This dealer almost never comes up with discounts this big. Now, TW’s Hobby64 line is slightly more expensive to get into, but I think it’s worth going for it if you want the coolest models possible for your collection.
DTM fans rejoice! Photo: Tarmac Works The new variation of the Audi R8 LMS GT3 evo II is a throwback to UNO Racing’s 24h of Spa challenge from 2023. The R8 has to be one of the most popular cars for the Hong Kong-based manufacturer, as you’ll find around 60 variations of it across multiple castings.
While you can only buy a maximum of three units of the UNO Racing Special Edition in pink (at $23.90 each), there’s no limit to how many replicas of the FIA GT World Cup 2025 you can get.
At $36.90 each, expect to find some Tarmac Cards inside as well. I’ve unboxed a few myself this year, but it’s not a direction I’m keen on pursuing for the future. Porsches are just as popular in the Tarmac Works Universe, and I’m not just talking about RWB collectibles. There are three different castings for the 911 GT3 R, starting with the older ones all the way up to the 992.
You’ll find a Falken-powered one in each category, and for the latest drop we’re looking at the #33 car which I saw live at last year’s 24H Nurburgring event . Neither one of the team’s cars managed to finish the race sadly, but this is still an iconic machine nonetheless. If you must have something with a proven record behind it, I’m sure Ayhancan Güven’s DTM winner will satisfy that need.
Takumi switched to a Mercedes? Photo: Tarmac Works As much as I love Initial D, seeing the black and white livery on a Mercedes-AMG GT3 does nothing for me and I’ll easily skip both the Bathurst 12h 2026 and the Shanghai 8 Hours variations.
The Jever Racing livery is a bit more exciting on a Porsche 911 GT1 than it is on an Audi A4, but I’d still buy the latter if only for all the years I spent driving Audis around Europe for motorsports events.
Also, this reminds me that the 911 GT1 is part of TW’s Hobby64+ series, which currently only features three castings (Ford RS200 and Lancia 037 Rally). The Toy Story LB-KAIDO WORKS R32 Skyline is another item I will ignore, and I wonder if I can ever feel that way about the F40 GT.
It’s not even my favorite Ferrari ever, and I would still happily hunt for every one of the seven other variations on the market (plus the GTE!). You see, we’re really living in a golden age for collecting diecast models!
